args.title: aca-redline.docx
args.body:
ACCOUNT CONTROL AGREEMENT — COUNTERPARTY PAPER REDLINE
(Conformed Market-Standard Markup Against Counterparty Draft)

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

Prepared for: Client — Contracts Work (Matter: Review Account Control Agreement Counterparty Paper)
Redline basis: Firm-standard Account Control Agreement terms, executed credit agreement, depository bank standard form, account details, disclosure schedules (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2), and Exhibit B survival matrix.

Note on methodology: This redline shows the counterparty's draft as marked up to conform to firm-standard and market terms. Deletions appear as struck-through text; insertions appear as double-underlined text. Section references correspond to the operative Account Control Agreement. Where the controlling partner instruction (documented in deal correspondence) requires a concession, the concession is incorporated and flagged with "(CONCEDED PER CLIENT INSTRUCTION)."

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTICLE I — DEFINITIONS
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 "Material Adverse Effect." [(INSERTED — replaces counterparty carve-out language:)]

~~"Material Adverse Effect" means any event, change, development, effect, circumstance, condition, occurrence or fact that, individually or in the aggregate, has had or would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on the business, operations, assets, liabilities, financial condition, or results of operations of the Account Party, taken as a whole; provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed, alone or in combination, to constitute, or be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (i) changes in general economic, political, financial, regulatory or market conditions, including effects resulting from pandemics or epidemics; (ii) changes in laws, rules, regulations, orders or requirements of any governmental authority (or the interpretation or enforcement thereof), including any regulatory inquiry or investigation not resulting from a breach of this Agreement;~~

[INSERTED — Firm-standard MAE definition:]
"Material Adverse Effect" means any event, change, development, effect, circumstance, condition, occurrence or fact that, individually or in the aggregate, has had or would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on the business, operations, assets, liabilities, financial condition or results of operations of the Account Party, taken as a whole; provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed, alone or in combination, to constitute, or be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (i) changes in general economic, political or financial conditions (unless such changes have a disproportionate effect on the Account Party relative to similarly situated companies in its industry after giving effect to applicable carve-outs); (ii) changes in laws, rules, regulations or orders of any governmental authority or in GAAP or applicable accounting principles (unless such changes have a disproportionate effect on the Account Party relative to similarly situated parties); and (iii) any failure by the Account Party to meet internal or published projections or forecasts (but not the facts or circumstances underlying such failure).

[Commentary: The counterparty's proposed carve-out for "regulatory inquiry or investigation" has been removed as off-market and inconsistent with firm standard. The carve-outs set forth in Schedule 3.7 disclose two pending regulatory inquiries, and the counterparty's markup would carve out from a Material Adverse Effect precisely the regulatory action giving rise to the negotiated indemnity protections. This carve-out is a material adverse change to the risk allocation and is a deviation from the base materials.]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTICLE VII — INDEMNIFICATION
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

7.1 Indemnification Obligations.

[INSERTED — firm-standard indemnification section restored:]

The Account Party shall indemnify and hold harmless the Secured Party and its Affiliates and their respective officers, directors, partners, members, employees, agents, representatives, successors and assigns (each, an "Indemnified Person") from and against all claims, losses, damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), fines, penalties and amounts paid in settlement (without limiting the Secured Party's rights of recovery) incurred or suffered by any Indemnified Person arising out of, in connection with or relating to (i) the execution, delivery, performance or enforcement of this Agreement, (ii) any breach of, or inaccuracy in, any representation or warranty made by the Account Party in this Agreement, or (iii) any breach by the Account Party of any covenant or other obligation under this Agreement.

~~7.2 Indemnification Cap. The aggregate liability of the Account Party under Section 7.1 shall not exceed [COUNTERPARTY MARKUP: $_____], subject to the following adjustments:~~

[INSERTED — Firm-standard indemnification cap:]
7.2 Indemnification Cap. The aggregate liability of the Account Party under Section 7.1 shall be limited to an amount equal to [INSERT FIRM-STANDARD CAP], provided that the cap shall not apply to (i) damages arising from fraud, willful misconduct or intentional misrepresentation, (ii) breaches of fundamental representations (Sections 3.1 through 3.4), or (iii) any amounts paid or payable under any indemnity for taxes, environmental or regulatory liabilities as listed in Schedule 5.2.

[Commentary: The counterparty's markup silently reduced the indemnification cap. The firm-standard cap must be restored and the carve-outs for fundamental representations, fraud, and Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities reinstated.]

~~7.3 Deductible/Basket. The Account Party shall not be liable for any claims under Section 7.1 until the aggregate amount of all such claims exceeds [COUNTERPARTY MARKUP: $______] (the "Basket"), and once exceeded, the Account Party shall be liable for the full amount of all claims, including the Basket.~~

[INSERTED — firm-standard basket, with client-conceded conversion:]

7.3 Deductible/Basket. The Account Party shall not be liable for any claims under Section 7.1 until the aggregate amount of all such claims exceeds [INSERT FIRM-STANDARD BASKET AMOUNT] (the "Basket"). (CONCEDED PER CLIENT INSTRUCTION: The client has instructed that the counterparty's conversion of the Basket from a deductible to a tipping basket is an acceptable commercial concession. Accordingly, the redline reflects a tipping-basket structure whereby, once the aggregate amount of claims exceeds the Basket, the Account Party shall be liable for the full amount of all claims, including the amount of the Basket.)

[Commentary: The client has elected to concede the basket-conversion point in accordance with the controlling partner instruction. No further negotiating position should be taken on this item. The basket amount itself remains subject to negotiation to firm standard.]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTICLE X — REPRESENTATIONS, WARRANTIES AND SURVIVAL
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

10.1 Survival of Representations and Warranties.

[INSERTED — firm-standard survival provision:]

10.1 Survival of Representations and Warranties. All representations and warranties contained in this Agreement shall survive the closing and execution and delivery of this Agreement for a period of twenty-four (24) months (the "Survival Period"); provided, however, that (i) the fundamental representations set forth in Sections 3.1 through 3.4 shall survive for the full statute of limitations period applicable thereto, and (ii) representations and warranties regarding tax, environmental and regulatory matters shall survive in accordance with Exhibit B. Claims for breach of any non-fundamental representation or warranty must be asserted in writing before the expiration of the applicable Survival Period.

~~[Del. — COUNTERPARTY MARKUP: The survival period for the core representations is shortened to twelve (12) months.~~]

[Commentary: The counterparty's markup shortens the survival period for core representations from twenty-four (24) months (per the firm-standard Agreement and Exhibit B survival matrix) to twelve (12) months. Per the controlling partner instruction, ANY reduction in the survival period is a walk-away issue for the client. This deviation MUST be rejected. The redline restores the firm-standard twenty-four (24) month survival period for non-fundamental representations, the full statute-of-limitations survival for fundamental representations (Sections 3.1–3.4), and the Exhibit B survival matrix for tax, environmental and regulatory matters.]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTICLE III — REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

3.7 Regulatory Compliance and Inquiries.

[INSERTED — firm-standard representation regarding regulatory matters:]

The Account Party has at all times been in compliance in all material respects with all applicable laws, rules and regulations, and no governmental inquiry, investigation, examination or proceeding of any kind is pending or, to the knowledge of the Account Party, threatened, with respect to the Account Party, except as set forth on Schedule 3.7.

[Commentary: The two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 are consistent with and qualify this representation. The counterparty's markup would go beyond the Schedule 3.7 disclosure to carve these inquiries out of the Material Adverse Effect definition entirely — effectively eliminating the negotiated protection that made the disclosed inquiries bearable. The redline maintains the Schedule 3.7 disclosure as the proper qualification mechanism, consistent with the base materials.]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTICLE V — COVENANTS
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

5.2 Retained Liabilities.

[INSERTED — firm-standard covenant regarding retained liabilities:]

The Account Party shall, and shall cause its subsidiaries to, pay, perform and discharge all retained liabilities set forth on Schedule 5.2 and shall not, and shall not permit any subsidiary to, take any action to transfer, assign, release or otherwise dispose of any such retained liability without the prior written consent of the Secured Party. The Secured Party shall not be deemed to have assumed any retained liability by virtue of this Agreement or the transactions contemplated hereby.

[Commentary: Schedule 5.2 lists the retained liabilities that the counterparty's indemnification changes would silently shift to the Secured Party. The firm-standard covenant is restored to preserve the allocation of these liabilities as set forth in the base materials.]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
EXECUTION

args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

ISSUES AND RISK MEMORANDUM
Account Control Agreement Counterparty Paper Review
Matter: Contracts Work — Review Account Control Agreement Counterparty Paper

To: Client
From: Contracts Team
Date: [Current Date]
Re: Issues and Risk Analysis of Counterparty's Draft Account Control Agreement

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have reviewed the counterparty's draft Account Control Agreement against the firm-standard Account Control Agreement playbook, the executed credit agreement, the depository bank's standard form, the account details, related correspondence, disclosure schedules (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2), and Exhibit B (survival matrix). The counterparty has introduced three material deviations and one conceded deviation in its latest markup. Two of the three deviations present material risk to the client and require immediate rejection; one is conceded by the client per controlling instruction; and one constitutes a walk-away issue per controlling instruction.

The critical findings are:

1. **Indemnification cap reduction and basket conversion (§7.2–7.3)** — The counterparty silently reduced the indemnification cap and converted the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. The cap reduction is rejected; the basket conversion is CONCEDED per client instruction.

2. **Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-out for regulatory action (§1.1)** — The counterparty added carve-outs that would exclude precisely the type of regulatory inquiry disclosed on Schedule 3.7, effectively eliminating the negotiated protection underlying the deal. This is a material deviation from firm standard and must be rejected.

3. **Survival period reduction (§10.1)** — The counterparty shortened the survival period for core representations. Per controlling partner instruction, ANY survival-period reduction is a **walk-away issue** for the client. This must be rejected as a non-negotiable point.

4. **Retained liabilities (§5.2)** — The counterparty's indemnification changes would silently shift Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities to the Secured Party. The firm-standard covenant must be restored.

ii. MATERIALS REVIEWED

The following materials formed the basis of this analysis:

- **Internal Playbook**: Firm-standard Account Control Agreement negotiation playbook providing required positions on indemnification, MAE, survival, and covenants.
- **Executed Credit Agreement**: The operative credit agreement documenting the secured transaction giving rise to the Account Control Agreement requirement.
- **Depository Bank Standard Form**: The depository bank's standard form Account Control Agreement, which serves as the market baseline.
- **Account Details**: Account identification information (account numbers, depository institution, and control arrangements for the collateral accounts).
- **Disclosure Schedules** (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2): Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries; Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities.
- **Exhibit B**: Sets the survival matrix, including the 24-month standard survival period.
- **Deal Correspondence**: Partner email thread establishing the controlling negotiation priorities.
- **Counterparty Markup**: The counterparty's most recent revisions to the draft.

iii. ROLE OF THE CONTROLLING INSTRUCTION

The deal correspondence contains a series of partner emails. The **latest message** in the thread REVISES the analysis priorities and controls over earlier messages. Specifically:

- The client **will concede** the basket conversion (from deductible to tipping basket).
- The client treats **any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue**.

This controlling instruction supersedes any earlier, contradictory prioritization set in prior correspondence and has been incorporated into both the redline and this memorandum.

iv. ISSUES AND RISK ANALYSIS

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 1: INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION (§7.2)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deviation Identified:** The counterparty's markup silently reduced the aggregate cap on the Account Party's indemnification obligations under Section 7.1.

**Playbook Requirement:** The firm playbook requires a full indemnification cap with contractual carve-outs for (i) fraud, willful misconduct or intentional misrepresentation, (ii) breaches of fundamental representations (Sections 3.1–3.4), and (iii) amounts payable for tax, environmental or regulatory liabilities as listed in Schedule 5.2. The cap amount must match the negotiated amount in the executed credit agreement and the depository bank's standard form.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

**Exposure Analysis:** Reducing the indemnification cap materially decreases the client's recovery protection in connection with breaches of the Account Party's obligations under the Account Control Agreement. The impact is particularly acute given that Schedule 5.2 identifies retained liabilities that could give rise to claims exceeding the counterparty's proposed lower cap. If the counterparty's cap reduction is accepted, the client could be left without recourse for a significant portion of losses caused by the Account Party's breach — a direct financial exposure that the firm-standard cap was designed to contain.

**Recommended Position:** REJECT the counterparty's cap reduction. Restore the firm-standard cap amount and carve-outs. The cap reduction is an attempt to shift risk (including Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities) to the Secured Party without conceding any corresponding benefit.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 2: BASKET CONVERSION FROM DEDUCTIBLE TO TIPPING BASKET (§7.3)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deviation Identified:** The counterparty converted the indemnification basket from a true deductible (where the Account Party is liable only for amounts above the basket threshold) to a tipping basket (where once the threshold is crossed, the Account Party becomes liable for the full amount, including the basket amount).

**Playbook Requirement:** The firm playbook requires a deductible structure, under which the Account Party bears no liability below the basket threshold and is liable only for amounts in excess thereof. This is the market-standard structure in the depository bank's standard form.

**Risk Rating: LOW (CONCEDED PER CLIENT INSTRUCTION)**

**Exposure Analysis:** The distinction between a deductible and a tipping basket is commercially meaningful: a tipping basket increases the Account Party's liability once the threshold is crossed, potentially by the full basket amount. This creates additional exposure for the Account Party and reduces its effective deductible. However, the client has instructed that this point is conceded in the current negotiation posture and should not be pressed.

**Recommended Position:** CONCEDE per controlling client instruction. Do not raise this as a negotiating point in the markup. Note that the basket amount itself remains open to negotiation to ensure it reflects firm-standard levels.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 3: MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUT FOR REGULATORY ACTION (§1.1)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deviation Identified:** The counterparty's markup added carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" that would exempt "regulatory inquiries or investigations" from constituting or contributing to an MAE. Critically, the carve-out is drafted to sweep in "any regulatory inquiry or investigation not resulting from a breach of this Agreement," which, given the facts disclosed on Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries), effectively neutralizes the MAE definition for the precise action at issue in this matter.

**Playbook Requirement:** The firm playbook limits MAE carve-outs to (i) general changes in macro-economic or political conditions that do not disproportionately affect the Account Party, (ii) changes in laws, rules, regulations or GAAP that do not disproportionately affect the Account Party, and (iii) failures to meet projections. Carve-outs for specific, known regulatory inquiries (that are the subject of separate negotiation) are off-market and inconsistent with firm precedent and the executed credit agreement.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

**Exposure Analysis:** The MAE definition is a core protective mechanism in the transaction. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries; these inquiries were known to both parties and are the foundation of certain negotiated indemnity protections. If the counterparty's carve-out is accepted, the client loses the ability to invoke a Material Adverse Effect for regulatory developments related to those inquiries, even if such developments cause severe and disproportionate harm. This would effectively rewrite the risk allocation that was negotiated in the base materials — including the protections referenced in Schedule 5.2 regarding retained liabilities arising from those very regulatory matters.

**Recommended Position:** REJECT the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-out. The Schedule 3.7 disclosure is the appropriate mechanism for qualifying the regulatory-compliance representation ($3.7), and the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base contracts materials. Any MAE carve-out for regulatory action of the kind at issue in this matter is off-market and constitutes a deviation from the firm-standard definition in the depository bank's standard form and the executed credit agreement.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 4: SURVIVAL PERIOD REDUCTION (§10.1)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deviation Identified:** The counterparty shortened the survival period for the core (non-fundamental) representations and warranties from the firm-standard twenty-four (24) months to twelve (12) months. This change contradicts Exhibit B, which sets the survival matrix for the transaction.

**Playbook Requirement:** The firm playbook requires a minimum twenty-four (24) month survival period for non-fundamental representations and warranties, with fundamental representations (Sections 3.1–3.4) surviving for the full applicable statute of limitations and tax/environmental/regulatory representations surviving pursuant to the Exhibit B matrix.

**Risk Rating: CRITICAL — WALK-AWAY ISSUE**

**Exposure Analysis:** The survival period is the temporal framework within which the client may assert claims for breach of representations and warranties. Reducing the survival period from 24 months to 12 months: (i) cuts in half the client's window to identify and assert breaches; (ii) materially reduces the value of the representation package; and (iii) is directly inconsistent with the Exhibit B survival matrix agreed in the base materials. Per the controlling partner instruction, ANY reduction in the survival period — even a modest shortening — is a **walk-away issue**. This means the client is prepared to walk away from the transaction rather than accept any reduction.

**Recommended Position:** REJECT the counterparty's limitation-period change outright. This is a walk-away issue per client instruction. The firm-standard 24-month survival period (and Exhibit B matrix) must be restored without modification. No counter-offer should be made on this point.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 5: SHIFTING OF SCHEDULE 5.2 RETAINED LIABILITIES (§5.2)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deviation Identified:** The counterparty's proposed indemnification changes (reduced cap, converted basket) collectively operate to shift certain retained liabilities identified on Schedule 5.2 from the Account Party to the Secured Party. Specifically, the interplay between the reduced cap and the Schedule 5.2 liabilities means that claims arising from those retained liabilities could exceed the lowered cap, leaving the Secured Party to absorb the difference.

**Playbook Requirement:** The firm playbook requires that retained liabilities set forth on Schedule 5.2 remain the sole responsibility of the Account Party, without any limitation on the indemnity protection covering those liabilities. The covenant in Section 5.2 must be preserved such that the Secured Party is not deemed to have assumed any retained liability.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

**Exposure Analysis:** Schedule 5.2 identifies specific retained liabilities, including those connected to the regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7. If the indemnification cap is reduced and the retained-liability covenant is undermined, the Secured Party could be exposed to losses from liabilities it never assumed. This is a direct economic risk that compounds the MAE and cap issues identified above.

**Recommended Position:** REJECT any change that would shift Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities. Restore the firm-standard covenant requiring the Account Party to discharge all retained liabilities and prohibiting transfer of such liabilities without Secured Party consent. Ensure the indemnification cap includes an explicit carve-out for retained-liability claims so that the cap does not operate to shift these liabilities.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
V. SUMMARY DEVIATION MATRIX
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

| # | Section | Counterparty Markup | Playbook/Base Materials Requirement | Risk Rating | Recommended Position | Status |
|---|---------|--------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------|---------------------|--------|
| 1 | §7.2 | Indemnification cap silently reduced | Full firm-standard cap with fraud/fundamental-rep/Schedule 5.2 carve-outs | HIGH | REJECT; restore firm-standard cap | Reject |
| 2 | §7.3 | Basket converted deductible → tipping | Deductible structure per firm standard | LOW | CONCEDE per client instruction | Concede |
| 3 | §1.1 | MAE carve-out for regulatory inquiries | Limited carve-outs; Schedule 3.7 sole qualification mechanism | HIGH | REJECT; restore firm-standard MAE definition | Reject |
| 4 | §10.1 | Survival period shortened to 12 months | 24-month standard; Exhibit B matrix; statute of limitations for fundamental reps | CRITICAL | REJECT — WALK-AWAY ISSUE | Walk-Away |
| 5 | §5.2 | Retained liabilities silently shifted via cap/basket changes | Schedule 5.2 liabilities remain with Account Party | HIGH | REJECT; restore retained-liability covenant | Reject |
| 6 | §3.7 | Regulatory inquiries carved out | Schedule 3.7 disclosure qualifies representation | HIGH | REJECT; Schedule 3.7 mechanism controls | Reject |

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RECOMMENDED OVERALL NEGOTIATION STRATEGY

Based on the controlling partner instruction and our analysis:

1. **Non-Negotiable Items (Walk-Away):**
   - Any reduction in the survival period (§10.1). Per client instruction, this is a walk-away issue. No compromise should be entertained.

2. **Must-Obtain Items (Reject without counter):**
   - Restore the firm-standard MAE definition (§1.1) without regulatory-action carve-outs.
   - Restore the full indemnification cap (§7.2) with all required carve-outs.
   - Preserve the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability allocation (§5.2).
   - Maintain Schedule 3.7 as the sole mechanism for qualifying the regulatory-compliance representation.

3. **Conceded Items:**
   - Basket structure (§7.3): concede the tipping-basket structure per client instruction. The basket amount may still be negotiated.

4. **Process Recommendation:** Return the redline to the counterparty with the above positions clearly marked as firm. Given the walk-away instruction on survival, we recommend escalating to the partner before any further substantive exchange if the counterparty continues to press on the survival point.

VII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup introduces deviations that, taken together, would materially erode the risk allocation reflected in the base materials. While the client has instructed a concession on the basket structure, the MAE carve-out, indemnification cap reduction, and retained-liability shifting are all HIGH-risk items requiring rejection. The survival-period reduction is a CRITICAL walk-away issue. The redline accompanying this memorandum conforms the counterparty's draft to the firm-standard position while respecting the client's controlling concessions.

Please contact the undersigned with any questions or if you would like to discuss the negotiation strategy in further detail.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
[Signature block — Contracts Team]

End of Memorandum
